passage: Dhruv met Manoj at the film club in October, and they hit it off. Over coffee the first week, Dhruv told him he was nervous about his mid-term. Manoj said, "Same, I always freeze in exams." The next week Dhruv mentioned his parents were arguing a lot, and Manoj shared that his own grandfather was ill. Small, matched steps. By December Dhruv felt safe enough to say he sometimes doubted whether he was good enough for the course. Manoj was quiet for a moment, then said, "I think about that too. Thanks for saying it." Dhruv felt lighter, not exposed. He had noticed that Manoj also never rushed him or repeated it to others. He thought about the first friend he'd told everything in one go, who had drifted away, and smiled.

qa.q: In which month did Dhruv say he doubted whether he was good enough?
qa.a: He said it in December.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv feel lighter and not exposed after his December sharing?
qa.a: Manoj answered with something of his own, never rushed him and kept it private, so Dhruv felt his trust was returned.

qa.q: What might Dhruv do if Manoj stopped sharing back?
qa.a: He could slow down and share only small things until he sees whether Manoj comes back with his own, rather than risk more.

qa.q: How might Manoj have felt when Dhruv told him about his doubts?
qa.a: Manoj probably felt trusted and understood, since he replied that he thinks the same thing and thanked Dhruv.

grounding: Dhruv shares fears gradually and watches Manoj's reciprocity as trust grows.

passage:
"Can I tell you something?" Manoj said, closing his laptop in the library. Siddharth, who had known him a month, looked up from his notes.
"Sure."
"My dad lost his job last year. We nearly lost the house. I'm terrified I'll never get out of this, and my mother cries at night and I can hear her, and I still smile at everyone in class—"
Siddharth blinked. "That's... a lot. I'm glad you told me. I'm not sure what to say."
Manoj looked at the table. "Forget it. I don't know why I said all that."
"No, I mean it. Can we have chai and talk slower?"
Manoj nodded but his shoulders stayed tight. He wondered if he had said too much too fast.

qa.q: How long had Siddharth known Manoj?
qa.a: He had known him a month.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling after he said so much, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt exposed and unsure, since he told Siddharth to forget it, looked at the table and kept his shoulders tight.

qa.q: What could the two do now to rebuild comfort?
qa.a: They could have the chai and talk at a slower pace, with Siddharth sharing something of his own so the sharing feels more even.

qa.q: What is it like for Siddharth to hear so much so soon?
qa.a: Siddharth is caught off guard and doesn't know what to say, though he wants to be supportive, and asking to slow down shows he cares.

grounding: Manoj shares a lot too soon and feels exposed, showing why gradual matched sharing works better.

passage: Looking back at how Sarika and I became close in our first year, it happened slowly, and I think that's why it worked. I'm Zainab. At first we only talked about classes and hostel food. Then one night, after a bad test, I told her I was scared I'd been admitted by mistake. Just that. She didn't laugh. She said she felt the same about her English, and told me how kids teased her accent in school. A few weeks later, I told her a little more: that my father hadn't wanted me to study so far from home. She told me about her parents' divorce. Each time, it felt like we were both stepping forward together. I did once try to tell a girl from my lab everything about my family on the second day we met, and I felt so exposed afterwards that I avoided her for a week.

qa.q: What did Zainab first tell Sarika after a bad test?
qa.a: That Zainab was scared of having been admitted by mistake.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel after telling the lab girl everything on the second day?
qa.a: Zainab felt exposed and uncomfortable, avoiding her for a week afterwards.

qa.q: What made the friendship with Sarika feel safe?
qa.a: They shared gradually and matched each other, so each step of openness was met with a similar one.

qa.q: How did Sarika respond when Zainab first shared a fear?
qa.a: She didn't laugh and shared her own fear about her English and the teasing in school, which matched Zainab's openness.

grounding: Shows a young adult building trust through gradual, matched sharing, and feeling exposed after sharing too much too soon.

passage:
Peer-mentor programme coordinator's note, week two.
In today's small-group session, Jatin shared a great deal very quickly: his parents' fights, his breakup, a time he failed a year. The group was kind but quiet; no one shared much back. Payal, the peer mentor, noticed Jatin's face change afterwards. He went red and kept apologising, "Sorry, too much." After the session she sat with him. She told him nothing he said was wrong to feel, but that trust usually grows when people share bit by bit and see if others share back. She suggested he start with smaller things next week and watch how the group responds. Jatin said he felt embarrassed but also relieved someone had explained. I agree with Payal's approach and will check in with Jatin next week. I've also reminded mentors to open each session with lighter sharing before deeper topics.
— Farida

qa.q: What did Jatin share in the session?
qa.a: His parents' fights, his breakup, a time he failed a year.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel after sharing so much?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and exposed, going red and apologising, and later also relieved when Payal explained.

qa.q: What did Payal suggest to Jatin?
qa.a: To share bit by bit and watch whether others share back, starting with smaller things next week.

qa.q: How might the group have felt during Jatin's sharing?
qa.a: They were kind but quiet, perhaps unsure how to respond to so much so soon, which is why no one shared much back.

grounding: Shows a young adult who shared too much too soon feeling exposed, and a mentor explaining that trust grows through gradual, matched sharing.

passage:
Tuesday, late.
Three months with Nitin. Tonight on the terrace I told him the thing I haven't told anyone outside my family: that I stammered badly till I was fourteen and used to hide in the school toilet during roll call. My heart was thumping. I kept watching his face.
He didn't make a joke. He just listened. Then, after a while, he said he'd never told anyone that his older brother used to hit him, and that it's why he goes quiet when people shout. I didn't know that. I held his hand.
It feels different now, closer, like we both put something on the table. I'm glad I didn't tell him this in our first week, when I almost did. I don't think either of us would have been ready.
— Chandrika

qa.q: How long has Chandrika been with Nitin?
qa.a: Three months.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling while telling Nitin about the stammer?
qa.a: Chandrika was nervous, heart thumping and watching his face, and then felt closer and relieved when he listened.

qa.q: What made this moment of sharing work?
qa.a: It came after three months of trust, and Nitin listened and shared something of his own, so the openness was matched.

qa.q: How did Nitin respond to Chandrika's story?
qa.a: He listened without joking, then shared his own painful history about his older brother, matching Chandrika's openness.

grounding: Shows a young adult sharing vulnerability gradually with a partner and the partner reciprocating, which builds intimacy.
